\chapter{Naming a Date, and the Stretches Around It}
\label{ch:la-fecha-y-el-siglo}
\hlchaptermodality{343}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la fecha, el calendario, proximo, la epoca and el siglo, and say why a calendar began as a moneylender's account book.}

Complete ES-C343-siglo: name a date, find it on a calendar, point at the next one, and name the age it sits in.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la fecha]{la fecha — the date, from the line at the foot of a letter}

\label{lesson:ES-C343-fecha}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the timetable}, then \emph{the small hours}. (\emph{El horario}; \emph{la madrugada}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item los meses — what a date names.
  \item la semana — the other unit a date sits in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FE-cha}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{ch} is one sound, as in English \emph{church}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la fecha} — \textquotedblleft{}the date.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{facta} meant \emph{done, made} — the feminine past participle of \textbf{facere}, \emph{to do}.

The date meaning came off the bottom of letters. A scribe finished a document and wrote \textbf{facta in...} — \emph{done at} such a place on such a day. The word sitting where the day was written slowly became the name of the day itself. Spanish still says \textbf{fecha en Madrid} in formal documents, which is the original line, unchanged.

English did exactly the same trick with a different Latin word: \textbf{date} is \emph{data}, \emph{given}, from the \emph{datum} that closed a Roman letter. Two languages, two closing formulas, both promoted to mean the day.

\emph{Facere} is one of the biggest roots in English. A \textbf{fact} is a thing done. A \textbf{feat} is a deed. A \textbf{factory} makes things. \textbf{Perfect} is thoroughly made. And to \textbf{affect} something is to do something to it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A day can now be named, not merely lived through.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la fecha}
  \item \emph{¿cuál es la fecha?}
  \item \emph{la fecha de hoy}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{facta} mean? (Done, made.) And where in a letter did the word sit? (At the foot — \emph{done at} such a place, on such a day.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el calendario]{el calendario — the calendar, which began as a debt ledger}

\label{lesson:ES-C343-calendario}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the small hours}, then \emph{the date}. (\emph{La madrugada}; \emph{la fecha}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item los meses — what it is divided into.
  \item el horario — the same -ario ending.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ka-len-DA-rio}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{l} is bright and forward, and \emph{-rio} glides as one. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el calendario} — \textquotedblleft{}the calendar.\textquotedblright{}

Three layers, and none of them is a wall chart.

Start at the bottom with Latin \textbf{calāre}, \emph{to call out, to proclaim}. In early Rome a priest watched for the new moon and then called it out to the city — that was the announcement that a month had begun.

The day he called became the \textbf{Calendae}, the first of the month. And the first of the month was the day debts fell due, so the book in which a Roman moneylender wrote what he was owed was his \textbf{calendārium} — his \emph{first-of- the-month book}. An account ledger.

The ledger, not the moon, is what gave English its word. A \textbf{calendar} is a debt book that grew into a chart of days. The ending is the \textbf{-ario} you met in \emph{horario}: a thing to do with the calends.

The calling-out survives in \textbf{intercalate}, to call an extra day into the year — which is what a leap year does.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Days can be found, and now they can be kept.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el calendario}
  \item \emph{en el calendario}
  \item \emph{la fecha en el calendario}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{calendarium} in Rome? (An account book.) And why were the calends called that? (From \emph{calāre} — a priest called out the new moon.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[próximo]{próximo — next, which is only a way of saying nearest}

\label{lesson:ES-C343-proximo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the date}, then \emph{the calendar}. (\emph{La fecha}; \emph{el calendario}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cerca — the other way of saying near.
  \item la semana — what this most often marks.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PROK-si-mo}, the weight on the first beat, which is why it takes a written accent. The \emph{pr} is one quick cluster. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{próximo} — \textquotedblleft{}next,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}nearest.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{prope} meant \emph{near}. Its superlative \textbf{proximus} meant \emph{nearest} — the very closest of all.

Nothing in that is about time. Spanish borrowed the distance word to do time, which is what almost every language does: \textbf{la próxima semana} is \emph{next week}, and what it says underneath is \emph{the nearest week}. English does the identical thing when it says \emph{the coming week} or \emph{close to Christmas}.

The nearness is loud in English. \textbf{Proximity} is nearness. To \textbf{approximate} is to come near the right answer. To \textbf{approach} is to come near. And to \textbf{reproach} somebody is to bring a thing near them again, up close, where they cannot avoid looking at it.

Spanish also uses \textbf{el prójimo}, from the same root, for \emph{one's neighbour} — the nearest person, the one you are told to love.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Time can be pointed forward.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{próximo}
  \item \emph{la próxima semana}
  \item \emph{el próximo día}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{proximus} mean? (Nearest.) And what does \emph{next week} say underneath? (The nearest week.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la época]{la época — the age, named for a stopping point}

\label{lesson:ES-C343-epoca}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the calendar}, then \emph{next, nearest}. (\emph{El calendario}; \emph{próximo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la fecha — the small version of this.
  \item el calendario — where both are kept.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{E-po-ka}, the weight on the first beat, which is why it takes a written accent. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la época} — \textquotedblleft{}the age,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the era,\textquotedblright{} and in everyday speech \textquotedblleft{}the season\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}the time of year.\textquotedblright{}

This one is Greek, not Latin. \textbf{Epokhē} meant \emph{a stopping, a halt, a holding back}, from \textbf{epekhein} — \emph{to hold back}.

Astronomers gave it the meaning it now has. To measure where the stars are, you must first stop the clock at some agreed instant and reckon everything from there. That fixed instant was the \textbf{epoch}, the point where time was held still. From \emph{the moment we stopped the clock} it drifted to \emph{the stretch of time that moment opens}, which is what both Spanish and English mean by it now.

English kept the word almost unchanged as \textbf{epoch}. Greek \emph{epekhein} is also the root of \textbf{epoché} in philosophy, the deliberate suspension of judgement — holding your opinion back, which is the older sense doing its original job.

In daily Spanish it is far less grand than in English: \textbf{en esta época del año} is no more than \emph{at this time of year}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Stretches of time, not merely points in it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la época}
  \item \emph{en esta época}
  \item \emph{la época del año}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{epokhē} mean in Greek? (A stopping, a halt.) And why did astronomers need one? (To fix the instant they measured everything from.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el siglo]{el siglo — the century, and why secular means worldly}

\label{lesson:ES-C343-siglo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{next, nearest}, then \emph{the age, the era}. (\emph{Próximo}; \emph{la época}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la época — the vaguer stretch beside this exact one.
  \item los meses — the smaller divisions.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SI-glo}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{gl} is one cluster, and the \emph{g} is hard. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el siglo} — \textquotedblleft{}the century,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the age.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{saeculum} first meant \emph{a generation} — roughly the longest a person might live, and so \emph{an age of the world}. Romans held a festival, the \emph{ludi saeculares}, once per \emph{saeculum}, on the theory that nobody alive should have seen the last one.

Then the Church picked the word up and used it for a purpose it was never built for. Set against \textbf{eternity}, the \emph{saeculum} became \emph{this present world, the time we are stuck in} — as opposed to the world to come. A priest who lived among ordinary people rather than in a monastery was \emph{clerus saecularis}, clergy of this age.

That is where English \textbf{secular} comes from, and it explains a word that otherwise looks arbitrary. \textbf{Secular} does not mean \emph{non-religious} by any logic of its parts. It means \emph{belonging to this age} — and it drifted to mean worldly, then non-religious, one step at a time.

Spanish kept the plain arithmetic too: a \emph{siglo} is a hundred years, and \textbf{el siglo XXI} is the twenty-first century.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Ten words for placing a thing in time, from the minute to the century.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el siglo}
  \item \emph{el siglo XXI}
  \item \emph{hace un siglo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{saeculum} first mean? (A generation, a lifetime.) And why does \emph{secular} mean worldly? (It meant \emph{of this age}, set against eternity.)
\end{tcolorbox}
